Described in this chapter are drugs that reduce intestinal motility such as the opioid analogues diphenoxylate and loperamide, and adsorbents such as attapulgite and kaolin. Bulking agents (which include bran and ispaghula) have also been used for diarrhoea and for adjusting faecal con- sistency in patients with colostomies. Described in this chapter are Albumin Tannate, p.1704 Ispaghula, p.1737 Attapulgite, p.1709 Kaolin, p.1738 Bismuth Compounds, p.1710 Lidamidine, p.1740 Bran, p.1712 Loperamide, p.1741 Chalk, p.1716 Racecadotril, p.1765 Difenoxin, p.1723 Smectites, p.1771 Diphenoxylate, p.1724 Zaldaride, p.1778 Antiemetics Antiemetics are a diverse group of drugs used to treat or prevent nausea and vomiting, including that associated with cancer therapy, anaesthesia, and motion sickness (see below). The choice of drug depends partly on the cause of nausea and vomiting. For example, hyoscine or an antihistamine are used in motion sickness whereas dopamine antagonists (such as metoclopramide and domperidone) and serotonin 5-HT3-receptor antagonists (5-HT3 antagonists), such as ondansetron, are ineffective. Conversely, nausea and vom- iting associated with cancer chemotherapy is often hard to control and special regimens have been devised including the use of the 5-HT3 antagonists, dexamethasone, and, more recently, the neurokinin-1 receptor antagonist apre- pitant. Described in this chapter are Alizapride, p.1704 Granisetron, p.1733 Aprepitant, p.1708 Indisetron, p.1736 Azasetron, p.1709 Itopride, p.1737 Bromopride, p.1713 Mecloxamine Citrate, Cerium Oxalate, p.1715 p.1744 Clebopride, p.1722 Metoclopramide, p.1747 Difenidol, p.1723 Metopimazine, p.1750 Dolasetron, p.1725 Nabilone, p.1750 Domperidone, p.1726 Ondansetron, p.1756 Dronabinol, p.1728 Palonosetron, p.1759 Fosaprepitant, p.1732 Ramosetron, p.1765 Ginger, p.1732 Tropisetron, p.1777 Antisecretory drugs Antisecretory drugs are used in the treatment and prophy- laxis of peptic ulcer disease (below); some are also em- ployed
